s: A 24-year-old woman at 14 weeks' gestation by dates has vaginal bleeding and severe nausea. Her uterus is the size of a 20-week pregnancy, and serum hCG is 350,000 mIU/mL. Ultrasound shows an intrauterine mass with many small cystic spaces and no fetus. Both ovaries are enlarged by many thin-walled, fluid-filled cysts.
l: Which of the following best explains the ovarian findings?
e: Very high hCG from a complete mole overstimulates the theca cells of both ovaries, because hCG acts on the LH receptor. The ovaries fill with many-chambered **theca lutein cysts**. They are functional, not neoplastic, and they shrink on their own once the mole is removed and hCG falls. A corpus luteum cyst is a single cyst that forms after ovulation. A follicular cyst is a single simple cyst from a follicle that did not rupture. An endometrioma holds old blood from endometriosis. A mature cystic teratoma is a germ cell tumor with fat and calcification.

w.Corpus luteum cysts: A corpus luteum cyst is a single cyst that forms after ovulation and may bleed. It does not fill both ovaries with many chambers in response to hCG.
w.Follicular cysts: A follicular cyst comes from one follicle that failed to rupture. It is single, simple and one-sided, and very high hCG does not cause it.
w.Endometriomas: An endometrioma is a chocolate cyst of old blood from endometriosis, with cyclic pain. It is not a response to a molar pregnancy.
w.Mature cystic teratomas: A dermoid cyst is a benign germ cell tumor with fat, hair and calcification. It is usually one-sided and has nothing to do with hCG.

et: Very high hCG acting on theca cells
Resolve in one or two cycles
bl: Bilateral multiloculated ovarian cysts with very high hCG, as in a molar pregnancy, are theca lutein cysts that regress after evacuation.

hl: hCG very high, uterus large for dates
pt.say: The complete mole column pairs a very high hCG with theca lutein cysts: the hCG overstimulates the ovaries, so her enlarged, multicystic ovaries are theca lutein cysts.

s: A 23-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 2 hours after sudden right lower quadrant pain that began during intercourse. Her last menstrual period began 24 days ago, and her cycles are regular. She is afebrile, with blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg and pulse 92/min. Urine hCG is negative. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 3.5-cm right ovarian cyst with a lacy, reticular internal pattern, a small amount of free pelvic fluid, and normal arterial and venous Doppler flow to both ovaries.
l: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Pain in the second half of a regular cycle, a negative pregnancy test, and a cyst with a lacy pattern of clot plus a little free fluid fit a **hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst**. The corpus luteum is rich in vessels and bled into itself, and intercourse is a common trigger for rupture. Most cases settle with pain relief. Torsion is less likely with normal Doppler flow in a mildly enlarged ovary, although normal flow never rules it out completely. A negative hCG excludes ectopic pregnancy. A follicular cyst is anechoic. A tubo-ovarian abscess comes with fever and cervical motion tenderness.

w.Ovarian torsion: Torsion causes sudden severe pain with vomiting in a large ovary, often with lost venous flow. Here the ovary is only mildly enlarged and both venous and arterial flow are normal.
w.Ruptured ectopic pregnancy: A ruptured tubal pregnancy can cause pain and free fluid, but it needs a positive hCG. A negative urine test essentially rules it out.
w.Follicular cyst: A follicular cyst forms before ovulation and is thin walled and anechoic. A lacy clot pattern after day 14 points to a bleeding corpus luteum.
w.Tubo-ovarian abscess: A tubo-ovarian abscess follows pelvic inflammatory disease and brings fever, discharge, cervical motion tenderness and a thick-walled complex mass.

et: Enlarged edematous ovary, reduced venous flow
Adnexal mass, blood in the pelvis
bl: Luteal-phase pain after intercourse with a lacy, reticular cyst and a negative hCG is a hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst.

pt.say: The hemorrhagic cyst panel shows lace-like reticular echoes with no flow, matching her scan, so a bleeding corpus luteum cyst explains the sudden pain.

s: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after the sudden onset of severe left pelvic pain with repeated vomiting. She has had no fever. Her abdomen is tender in the left lower quadrant. Urine hCG is negative. Ultrasound shows a 7-cm left ovarian mass containing fat and a calcified focus, with an enlarged, edematous ovary and peripherally displaced follicles; color Doppler still shows arterial flow into the ovary.
l: Which vascular event occurs first in this condition?
o: Compression of thin-walled veins and lymphatics
Embolic occlusion of the uterine artery
Spasm of the internal iliac artery
Rupture of the ovarian capsule vessels
e: The mass with fat and calcification is a dermoid, and its weight twisted the ovary on its infundibulopelvic ligament. **Compression of the thin-walled veins** and lymphatics comes first, because their low pressure cannot resist the twist, while the muscular ovarian artery keeps pushing blood in. The trapped blood and lymph make the ovary swell with edema, which pushes the follicles to the edge and explains why Doppler can still show arterial flow. Only later do rising pressure and more twisting stop arterial inflow and cause hemorrhagic infarction. Arterial thrombosis, emboli and spasm are not how torsion begins.

w.Thrombosis of the ovarian artery: Arterial occlusion is the late event in torsion, after venous congestion raises tissue pressure. Her Doppler still shows arterial inflow, so the artery is open.
w.Embolic occlusion of the uterine artery: Embolization of the uterine artery is a deliberate treatment for fibroids and postpartum bleeding. Emboli are not how a twisted ovary loses its blood supply.
w.Spasm of the internal iliac artery: The internal iliac artery lies on the pelvic sidewall, away from the twisting pedicle. Vasospasm plays no part in ovarian torsion.
w.Rupture of the ovarian capsule vessels: Bleeding from capsule vessels is not how torsion begins. The first vascular event is compression of the veins.

et: Compression of thin-walled veins and lymphatics
Venous flow lost; arterial flow kept
Embolic occlusion of the uterine artery
Spasm of the internal iliac artery
Rupture of the ovarian capsule vessels
bl: In ovarian torsion, compression of thin-walled veins and lymphatics comes first, so arterial Doppler flow can persist early.

pt.say: Follow the second step: the thin-walled, low-pressure veins and lymphatics are compressed first while the thick-walled artery still pushes blood in, so her ovary swells before arterial flow stops.

s: A 35-year-old woman has palpitations, heat intolerance and a 5-kg weight loss over 3 months. Her pulse is 108/min and she has a fine tremor. The thyroid gland is not enlarged or tender, and there is no exophthalmos. Serum TSH is suppressed and free T4 is elevated, but the 24-hour radioactive iodine uptake over the neck is very low. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 6-cm complex left adnexal mass, and a whole-body scan shows intense iodine uptake in the pelvis. Serum hCG is normal.
l: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hyperthyroidism?
e: Hyperthyroidism with very low neck iodine uptake means the thyroid gland itself is not making the hormone. The intense pelvic uptake puts working thyroid tissue in the ovary. **Struma ovarii** is a teratoma made mostly of thyroid tissue. Choriocarcinoma can cause hyperthyroidism because very high hCG stimulates the TSH receptor, but that drives the thyroid gland itself, so neck uptake would be high, and her hCG is normal. Granulosa cell tumors make estrogen. Dysgerminomas raise LDH, and serous cystadenomas make no hormone.

w.Choriocarcinoma: Very high hCG can stimulate TSH receptors and cause hyperthyroidism, but then the thyroid gland itself would take up iodine avidly. Her hCG is normal.
w.Granulosa cell tumor: Granulosa cell tumors make estrogen and inhibin, causing endometrial hyperplasia and bleeding. They contain no thyroid follicles and do not take up iodine.
w.Dysgerminoma: Dysgerminoma is a germ cell tumor made of sheets of clear cells that raises LDH. It has no thyroid tissue and does not cause thyrotoxicosis.
w.Serous cystadenoma: A serous cystadenoma is a benign epithelial cyst that makes no hormone. It would not take up radioactive iodine.

et: Low; uptake is in the pelvis
hCG, which stimulates the TSH receptor
bl: Thyrotoxicosis with low neck uptake and iodine uptake in a pelvic mass means struma ovarii, a teratoma made of thyroid tissue.

hl: uptake sits in a pelvic teratoma
pt.say: In the low-uptake group, struma ovarii is the cause whose iodine uptake sits in a pelvic teratoma, matching her low neck uptake and intense pelvic uptake.

s: A 26-year-old woman has an incidental 5-cm left adnexal mass found on transvaginal ultrasound during evaluation of irregular bleeding. The mass contains a fat-fluid level, a bright echogenic nodule that casts an acoustic shadow, and a curved calcification shaped like a tooth. CA-125, AFP and hCG are normal.
l: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Fat, a bright nodule with an acoustic shadow (the dermoid plug) and a tooth-like calcification in a young woman with normal markers mean a **mature cystic teratoma**, or dermoid cyst. It is the most common ovarian neoplasm in young women. It holds mature tissue from all three germ layers, such as skin, hair, sebum, teeth and cartilage. It is benign, but its weight makes torsion a risk. An immature teratoma is usually solid and contains immature neuroepithelium. Dysgerminoma is a solid mass with raised LDH. An endometrioma holds old blood. A mucinous cystadenoma is a large, many-chambered cyst without fat or teeth.

w.Immature teratoma: Immature teratomas are malignant, mostly solid tumors of adolescents, with immature neuroepithelium. Fat and a tooth in a cyst mean mature tissue.
w.Dysgerminoma: Dysgerminoma is a solid mass of clear cells that often raises LDH. It contains no fat or teeth.
w.Endometrioma: An endometrioma is a chocolate cyst of old blood with uniform low-level echoes and cyclic pain. It has no fat or calcification.
w.Mucinous cystadenoma: A mucinous cystadenoma is a large, many-chambered cyst filled with thick mucin. It has no fat, hair or teeth.

bl: Fat, a shadowing nodule and a tooth in an adnexal cyst of a young woman mean a mature cystic teratoma, the dermoid cyst.

pt.say: In the germ cell column, the mature teratoma box names the dermoid with hair and teeth, which is exactly what her ultrasound shows.

s: A 17-year-old girl has 3 weeks of increasing abdominal girth and pelvic pressure. Examination shows a firm, 14-cm pelvic mass. Serum AFP is markedly elevated, and hCG and LDH are normal. The mass is removed; histology shows a reticular network of primitive cells with perivascular structures in which a central capillary is wrapped by tumor cells inside a space lined by more tumor cells.
l: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e: A fast-growing germ cell tumor in a young woman with a very high AFP and glomerulus-like structures (Schiller-Duval bodies) is a **yolk sac tumor**. Its cells imitate the embryonic yolk sac, which normally makes AFP, so the marker supports the diagnosis and tracks the response to treatment. Dysgerminoma raises LDH and forms sheets of clear cells. Choriocarcinoma raises hCG. An immature teratoma shows immature neuroepithelium. A juvenile granulosa cell tumor makes estrogen and inhibin, not AFP.

w.Dysgerminoma: Dysgerminoma forms sheets of clear fried-egg cells with lymphocyte-rich septa and raises LDH, not AFP.
w.Choriocarcinoma: Choriocarcinoma is made of trophoblast without villi and secretes hCG. It bleeds easily and spreads early to the lungs.
w.Immature teratoma: Immature teratoma contains immature neuroepithelium and mixed embryonic tissues, and AFP may rise only slightly. It lacks Schiller-Duval bodies.
w.Juvenile granulosa cell tumor: Juvenile granulosa cell tumors secrete estrogen and inhibin and can cause precocious puberty. They do not make AFP or form glomerulus-like bodies.

bl: A young woman's ovarian mass with a high AFP and Schiller-Duval bodies is a yolk sac tumor.

pt.say: The yolk sac tumor box in the germ cell column pairs Schiller-Duval bodies with AFP, exactly her histology and her marker.

s: A 17-year-old phenotypic girl is evaluated for primary amenorrhea. She is 170 cm tall, breast development is Tanner stage 1, and she has a normal uterus and vagina. FSH and LH are elevated, and karyotype is 46,XY. Imaging shows a solid 8-cm right gonadal mass. Serum LDH is markedly elevated, and AFP is normal. The mass consists of sheets of large cells with clear cytoplasm and central nuclei separated by fibrous septa full of lymphocytes.
l: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e: A 46,XY girl with a uterus, high gonadotropins and no breast development has Swyer syndrome: complete gonadal dysgenesis with streak gonads. Streak gonads that carry Y material have a high risk of germ cell tumors. Sheets of clear fried-egg cells with lymphocyte-rich septa and a high LDH define **dysgerminoma**, the ovarian counterpart of seminoma. Gonadoblastoma, its usual precursor, mixes germ cells with sex cord cells and calcifies. Yolk sac tumor raises AFP, choriocarcinoma raises hCG, and a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor makes androgens.

w.Yolk sac tumor: Yolk sac tumor raises AFP and shows Schiller-Duval bodies. Her AFP is normal, and the cells are uniform and clear.
w.Choriocarcinoma: Choriocarcinoma secretes hCG and is a hemorrhagic tumor of trophoblast without villi. Clear cells with lymphocyte-rich septa do not fit.
w.Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors secrete androgens and cause virilization. They form tubules and nests of Leydig cells, not sheets of clear germ cells.
w.Gonadoblastoma: Gonadoblastoma is the in situ precursor in dysgenetic gonads, with small nests of germ and sex cord cells and calcification. It is not a large solid mass with raised LDH.

et: Germ and sex cord cells with calcification
bl: A solid gonadal mass with raised LDH and clear cells in a 46,XY girl with streak gonads is a dysgerminoma.

pt.say: The dysgerminoma box pairs fried-egg clear cells with LDH, matching her histology and her markedly raised lactate dehydrogenase.

s: A 58-year-old woman has had vaginal bleeding for 1 month, 7 years after menopause. She takes no hormones. Endometrial biopsy shows atypical endometrial hyperplasia. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 7-cm solid right ovarian mass. At surgery the mass is yellow and solid; histology shows small cells with grooved nuclei arranged around tiny follicle-like spaces filled with eosinophilic material.
l: Which serum marker is most useful for following this patient after surgery?
e: Bleeding after menopause, endometrial hyperplasia, a solid ovarian mass, and coffee-bean nuclei around Call-Exner bodies describe an adult granulosa cell tumor. Its cells make estrogen, which stimulated the endometrium, and **inhibin**, the hormone granulosa cells normally release to suppress FSH. Inhibin tracks the tumor and rises with recurrence. CA-125 follows epithelial cancers. Alpha-fetoprotein follows yolk sac tumors, lactate dehydrogenase follows dysgerminoma, and beta-hCG follows choriocarcinoma.

w.CA-125: CA-125 comes from coelomic-type epithelium and follows epithelial ovarian cancer, especially high-grade serous carcinoma. It is not a reliable marker of sex cord-stromal tumors.
w.Alpha-fetoprotein: AFP is a yolk sac and fetal liver protein. It marks yolk sac tumors of young women, not granulosa cell tumors.
w.Lactate dehydrogenase: LDH is a nonspecific marker of cell turnover that tracks dysgerminoma. It does not follow hormone-making stromal tumors.
w.Beta-hCG: Beta-hCG marks choriocarcinoma and trophoblastic disease. Granulosa cells secrete estrogen and inhibin, not chorionic gonadotropin.

bl: Granulosa cell tumors make estrogen and inhibin, so inhibin is the marker used to follow them after surgery.

pt.say: The granulosa cell tumor box lists estrogen and inhibin: estrogen explains her bleeding, and inhibin is the marker to follow.

s: A 56-year-old woman has progressive shortness of breath and abdominal swelling. Chest x-ray shows a large right pleural effusion, and ultrasound shows ascites and a 10-cm solid right ovarian mass. CA-125 is mildly elevated. The mass is removed; it is firm and white, and histology shows bland spindle cells making abundant collagen. Over the next month the effusion and ascites resolve without further treatment.
l: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
e: A benign **fibroma** is made of bland, collagen-making spindle cells. With ascites and a right pleural effusion that disappear after the tumor is removed, this is Meigs syndrome. Fluid leaks from the tumor into the peritoneum and crosses the diaphragm to the chest. The mild CA-125 rise comes from irritated mesothelium, not cancer. A thecoma is made of lipid-filled cells and makes estrogen. A granulosa cell tumor makes estrogen and shows Call-Exner bodies. High-grade serous carcinoma would show malignant cells in the fluid and would not resolve after removal. A Krukenberg tumor contains signet-ring cells.

w.Thecoma: Thecomas are solid tumors of plump, lipid-filled cells that make estrogen and can cause bleeding. They are yellow, not firm and white with collagen.
w.Granulosa cell tumor: Granulosa cell tumors make estrogen and inhibin and show coffee-bean nuclei with Call-Exner bodies. They are not bland collagen-making spindle cell tumors.
w.High-grade serous carcinoma: Serous carcinoma causes malignant ascites, a markedly raised CA-125 and omental disease. Its effusions contain tumor cells and do not vanish after removing one ovary.
w.Krukenberg tumor: Krukenberg tumors are bilateral ovarian metastases of mucin-filled signet-ring cells, usually from the stomach. They are not bland spindle cell tumors.

bl: An ovarian fibroma with ascites and a right pleural effusion that resolve after removal is Meigs syndrome.

pt.say: The fibroma box in the sex cord-stromal column carries the label Meigs syndrome: fibroma, ascites and a right pleural effusion.

s: A 58-year-old woman has 3 months of abdominal bloating, early satiety and increasing abdominal girth. Examination shows shifting dullness and a fixed pelvic mass. CT shows ascites, bilateral complex adnexal masses and a thick sheet of tumor replacing the omentum. CA-125 is 1,200 U/mL. Biopsy of the omentum shows papillae of markedly atypical cells with frequent mitoses and scattered psammoma bodies. Her sister had breast cancer at 42.
l: Which statement best describes the origin and genetics of this tumor?
o: Tubal intraepithelial carcinoma with an early TP53 mutation
Serous borderline tumor with a KRAS or BRAF mutation
Endometriosis with a mismatch repair defect
Mucinous cystadenoma with a KRAS mutation
Surface inclusion cyst with PTEN loss
e: Bloating, early satiety, ascites, omental caking, bilateral masses and a very high CA-125, with highly atypical papillae and psammoma bodies, describe high-grade serous carcinoma. It usually begins as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma in the fimbriated end of the fallopian tube, with a **TP53 mutation** from the start. Her sister's early breast cancer suggests BRCA1 or BRCA2, which raise the risk of this type. Because it seeds the peritoneum early, most women present at an advanced stage. A serous borderline tumor with a KRAS or BRAF mutation is the slow path to low-grade serous carcinoma. Endometriosis leads to clear cell or endometrioid carcinoma, and mucinous tumors carry KRAS.

w.Serous borderline tumor with a KRAS or B: This is the type I path to low-grade serous carcinoma, which grows slowly and has mild atypia. Her tumor is highly atypical and has spread widely.
w.Endometriosis with a mismatch repair def: Cancers that arise in endometriosis are clear cell and endometrioid carcinomas, and they are usually found earlier. They do not usually cause omental caking.
w.Mucinous cystadenoma with a KRAS mutatio: Mucinous carcinomas arise from mucinous cystadenomas and borderline tumors with a KRAS mutation. They are large and usually one-sided, with no psammoma bodies.
w.Surface inclusion cyst with PTEN loss: Surface inclusion cysts were once blamed for serous cancer, but most high-grade serous carcinomas begin in the tube. PTEN loss is typical of endometrioid carcinoma.

et: Tubal intraepithelial carcinoma with an early TP53 mutation
Serous borderline tumor with a KRAS or BRAF mutation
Endometriosis with a mismatch repair defect
Mucinous cystadenoma with a KRAS mutation
Surface inclusion cyst with PTEN loss
bl: High-grade serous carcinoma arises from tubal intraepithelial carcinoma with an early TP53 mutation and spreads early over the peritoneum.

pt.say: The high-grade serous box reads tubal origin with TP53 and BRCA, the type II path that starts as tubal intraepithelial carcinoma.

s: A 49-year-old woman has 4 months of epigastric discomfort, early satiety and a 7-kg weight loss. Pelvic examination shows bilateral firm adnexal masses. Ultrasound shows two solid, enlarged ovaries with smooth surfaces. Biopsy of one ovary shows cells whose cytoplasm is distended by mucin, pushing the nucleus to one side, infiltrating a cellular ovarian stroma.
l: Which organ is the most likely primary site of this tumor?
e: Bilateral solid ovarian masses of mucin-filled signet-ring cells are a Krukenberg tumor, a metastasis most often from the **stomach**. Her upper abdominal pain, early satiety and weight loss point there. Bilateral masses are the clue that a mucinous ovarian tumor is metastatic, because primary mucinous tumors are usually large and one-sided. An appendiceal tumor typically causes pseudomyxoma peritonei, with pools of mucin. Pancreatic, colorectal and breast cancers are less common sources. Endometrial cancer can spread to the ovary but does not form signet-ring cells.

w.Appendix: Appendiceal mucinous tumors spread to the ovaries and peritoneum as pseudomyxoma peritonei, with gelatinous mucin and bland cells, not infiltrating signet-ring cells.
w.Ovary: Primary mucinous tumors of the ovary are usually large, cystic and one-sided. Bilateral solid ovaries full of signet-ring cells point to a metastasis.
w.Pancreas: Pancreatic cancer can spread to the ovaries, but it forms glands in dense stroma. It is a far less common source of Krukenberg tumors.
w.Endometrium: Endometrial cancer can spread to the ovary, but it forms glands and presents with bleeding after menopause. It does not form signet-ring cells.

bl: Bilateral solid ovarian masses of signet-ring cells are a Krukenberg tumor, usually metastatic from the stomach.

pt.say: The Krukenberg tumor box in the metastases column reads signet-ring cells from the stomach, the primary site in this case.

s: A 63-year-old woman, 12 years after menopause, has had pelvic pressure and mild bloating for 2 months. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 9-cm left adnexal mass with thick septations, a solid papillary component with internal Doppler flow, and a moderate amount of ascites. The right ovary is normal. CA-125 is 410 U/mL. She is otherwise healthy.
l: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Referral to a gynecologic oncologist for surgery
Laparoscopic cystectomy by a general gynecologist
Combined oral contraceptives to suppress the mass
CT-guided aspiration of the cyst fluid
e: A postmenopausal woman with a complex mass that has solid papillary tissue with flow, thick septations, ascites and a raised CA-125 is at high risk of ovarian cancer. Both the IOTA Simple Rules and O-RADS place her in the malignant category. **Referral to a gynecologic oncologist** is the next step, because a specialist surgeon removes the mass completely and stages it at the first operation, which improves survival. A repeat scan suits a simple cyst, not this mass. Cystectomy by a general gynecologist risks spilling the tumor and incomplete staging. Oral contraceptives do not shrink neoplasms. Puncturing the cyst can spill cancer cells.

w.Repeat ultrasound in 6 to 8 weeks: A repeat scan after a short interval suits a simple or hemorrhagic cyst in a younger woman. Delaying care for a high-risk mass lets the cancer progress.
w.Laparoscopic cystectomy by a general gyn: Removing a likely cancer without proper staging risks rupture and an incomplete operation. Outcomes are better when a gynecologic oncologist operates first.
w.Combined oral contraceptives to suppress: Hormone suppression was once tried for functional cysts, and it has no effect on neoplasms. Estrogen-containing pills are also not appropriate for a woman well past menopause.
w.CT-guided aspiration of the cyst fluid: Cyst fluid cytology misses most cancers, and puncturing a malignant cyst can seed tumor cells into the peritoneum, so aspiration is avoided.

et: Referral to a gynecologic oncologist for surgery
Laparoscopic cystectomy by a general gynecologist
Combined oral contraceptives to suppress the mass
CT-guided aspiration of the cyst fluid
bl: A postmenopausal complex adnexal mass with solid papillary flow, ascites and a high CA-125 warrants referral to a gynecologic oncologist for surgery.

pt.say: The worrisome panel shows her features, and its plan line reads refer to a gynecologic oncologist, the right next step for this mass.
